tables.caption: Polite nonpast → dictionary/plain nonpast; the whole bounded inventory is translated below.
The clause comes before the noun it identifies; every row is translated below.
Commit to memory versus an existing memory; all whole forms are translated below.
Polite nonpast, past and negative; translations below.

grammar.note_en:
A dictionary form is the basic plain nonpast form listed for a verb. “Nonpast” covers present habits and future actions; it is not a past tense. The familiar ます form is polite. Here the narrative, library encounter and requests stay polite. Inside a clause that modifies a noun, use the explicitly taught plain nonpast, even when the whole sentence ends politely. The form changes are whole taught pairs: よみます → よむ: “read”; かります → かりる: “borrow”; もちます → もつ: “hold”; みます → みる: “look”; いきます → いく: “go”; かします → かす: “lend”; おきます → おく: “put down”; かきます → かく: “draw a line/map”; えがきます → えがく: “depict/draw a shape”; さがします → さがす: “search for”. Do not infer an unrestricted conjugation rule from this list. No plain negative, plain past, past relative, potential or plain ている clause is taught.

A noun-modifying clause is a small description placed immediately before a noun. It identifies which person, paper or place the sentence means. ほんをよむひと = “a person who reads books”; わたしがもつかみ = “the paper I hold”; めいさんがみるかみ = “the paper Mei looks at”; ほんをかりるところ = “a place where one borrows books”; かわをえがくひと = “a person who depicts the river”; わたしがさがすひと = “the person I search for”. There is no extra word corresponding to English “who/that/where,” and no の is inserted between the verb and the following noun. In ほんをよむひと, “a person who reads books,” the person is understood as the reader; を still marks the book inside the clause. In ゆいがもつかみ, “the paper Yui holds,” the paper is the understood object; が marks Yui as the subject INSIDE that clause. The whole phrase can then take は or を in the surrounding sentence. This is a bounded introduction to subject/object/place gaps, not a licence for plain past or negative relatives.

A description can identify a regular visitor without revealing a personal name. いつも means always/regularly in a routine. 本をかす人 lends the book; 本をかりる人 borrows it. A person merely holding a blue book is not yet identified by the narrower borrowing description. こんにちは is the polite daytime greeting “hello.” としょかん is a library; ところ is a place/location. うつし is a separate copy. The new copy, a fresh comparison drawing and the older exposed map are distinct pieces of paper.

おぼえます means commit something to memory/learn it. The result-state form おぼえています means remember/have it in memory; おぼえていません means do not remember it. These bounded whole state forms are first dated HERE; knowing chapter12’s ています did not teach every memory verb automatically. わすれます means forget, わすれました “forgot,” and わすれません “do not/will not forget.” Those last forms use earlier polite verb tense/negative patterns, not plain past/negative. The object remembered or forgotten takes を; an omitted topic/object can be supplied by context.

かく here introduces drawing a line/map. Its polite draw-sense forms かきます/かきました/かきません/かきませんでした are dated here. Earlier 書きます meant write lettering, not an automatic licence for the new draw meaning; the old word and card dates remain intact. えがきます/えがく focuses on depicting a shape/scene. The two drawing verbs overlap for concrete drawings; their English labels are not an exclusive distinction. えんぴつ is a pencil; かたち shape; せん a drawn line, distinct from the older price unit せん “one thousand.” さいご is the end/last part: in this map it names the final segment along the route, not proven chronological order of pen strokes.

Polite past dialogue can refer to last night’s completed reading and return of the borrowed tools; this does not introduce past noun-modifying clauses. Authored story readings cover familiar known-word spellings, including new 借/返/雨/外/見/絵. New semantic vocabulary remains kana.

The authorship question uses a bounded subject question: だれがちずをかきましたか means “Who drew the map?” が marks the unknown person doing the drawing, and かきました uses the familiar polite past. This question does not introduce a plain-past noun modifier. The role-description clauses in this chapter use the explicitly taught nonpast forms.
